item.title: Code Without Purpose
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: The problem isn't too much code. It's code without purpose.
item.content:encoded:
Time is finite in ways I can’t ignore. That changes which questions about code feel important.

I read a post arguing that the most valuable programming skill in 2026 is deleting code. The thesis: AI generates code faster than anyone can review it, so the real value is in curation and subtraction. Code is a liability, not an asset.

I agree with the observation. I disagree with the prescription.

The Thesis

The argument is straightforward. AI tools can produce entire modules in the time it takes to write a spec. Codebases are accumulating features nobody asked for, abstractions nobody needs, and boilerplate that exists because the model defaulted to verbosity. Teams that used to struggle to ship enough code now struggle with too much of it. In this world, the programmer’s role shifts from writer to editor. The most valuable activity becomes knowing what to cut.

I’ve seen this. Projects accumulate code the way attics accumulate boxes. Nobody remembers why half of it is there. It sits untouched for months, adding to the cognitive load, making every change harder to reason about. When you finally clear it out, nothing breaks and the rest becomes legible again. Code rot is real. AI accelerates it. The instinct to subtract is correct.

But subtraction is symptom treatment. The underlying problem isn’t volume. It’s that most code doesn’t know why it exists. It was written (or generated) to solve a local problem, it solved it or half-solved it, and then it sat there, disconnected from any larger purpose. Code without purpose is the thing that bloats. Deletion is the right instinct pointed at the wrong layer. The cause isn’t too much code. It’s too little intent.

What I Found Instead

I started building tools two years ago because I needed my personal data to survive even if I wasn’t around to maintain it. That’s the whole constraint. Whatever I build has to work without me.

The first tool was a conversation archiver. I had years of AI conversations across ChatGPT, Claude, and Copilot, hundreds of threads trapped in platforms that might not exist next decade. I needed them in formats that degrade gracefully. SQLite for structured queries. JSONL for streaming and interchange. Markdown for human reading. If the tool disappears, the data is still a file you can open with anything. If SQLite disappears, the JSONL is still searchable with grep. If everything disappears, the Markdown is still readable in a text editor. Each layer works independently.

Then I needed the same thing for bookmarks. Then ebooks. Then photos, email, medical records, notes. Each tool exists because the previous one exposed a gap. The medical record consolidator needed a way to share results securely without a server, which led to a client-side encryption tool. The whole collection needed a dead man’s switch, a way to ensure delivery if I couldn’t do it myself. The archive eventually needed something stranger: a way to respond to questions after I couldn’t, which led to a conversable persona assembled from the combined data.

None of this was planned as an ecosystem. I built the next thing I needed, and the next, and the next. At some point I looked back and realized they all pointed the same direction. This is a life project. Everything serves one purpose.

The Stack

Fifteen tools, one purpose: durable personal data that outlasts its creator.

Philosophy

  • longecho: The Long Echo specification. Self-describing data, durable formats, graceful degradation. Also the compliance validator and unified site builder.

Source Toolkits (domain data → durable archives)

  • ctk: AI conversation archive. Tree-structured storage, semantic search, longecho-compliant exports to Markdown and HTML.
  • memex: AI conversation knowledge base. MCP-first, SQL-queryable, self-contained HTML export with in-browser conversation replay.
  • btk: Bookmarks from browser exports. SQLite with hierarchical tags and content caching.
  • ebk: eBook library. Calibre-compatible, full-text search, AI-powered tagging.
  • ptk: Photos. SHA256 deduplication, AI annotation via Claude and Ollama, album management.
  • mtk: Email archives from IMAP and mbox. Relationship mapping, privacy controls, semantic search.
  • chartfold: Medical records from Epic, MEDITECH, and athenahealth. Consolidated SQLite with MCP server for Claude.
  • jot: Notes and journal. Plaintext Markdown with YAML frontmatter, CLI-first, designed for LLM integration.

Infrastructure

  • pagevault: Client-side AES-256-GCM encryption for any HTML file. No server, no backend.
  • posthumous: Federated dead man’s switch. TOTP check-ins, escalating alerts, automated triggers.
  • deets: Personal identity metadata. TOML-backed, local-first.
  • crier: Cross-posting to dev.to, Bluesky, Mastodon, Hashnode. One source, many platforms.
  • repoindex: Git repository collection index. Tracks and queries across ~120 repos.

The Endgame

  • longshade: A conversable persona assembled from all archived data. Not resurrection. An echo.

The Pattern

Every tool in that list uses the same materials. SQLite for structured queries. JSONL for streaming and interchange. Markdown for human reading. Every tool includes a README that explains its own data format. Every database is a self-contained file you can copy to a USB drive, query from any programming language, or hand to someone who has never heard of the tool that created it.

The self-description matters. If you find one of these databases in twenty years, the README tells you what you’re looking at. The schema is in the file. The data doesn’t depend on an API or a cloud service or a company’s continued existence. It’s just a file that describes itself.

Most of these tools follow the same architecture: SQLite storage, CLI for local use, MCP server for Claude, export to self-contained HTML you can host on any static site or open from a file. Memex is a good example. Import your AI conversations, query them with SQL, talk to Claude about them via MCP, or export the whole thing as a single HTML file with embedded JavaScript that lets you browse and even continue conversations in the browser. Download the SQLite database from that same HTML file, and you’re back to durable local data. The cycle closes. This is how most of the tools work.

The dependency flow:

Source toolkits (ctk, memex, btk, ebk, ptk, mtk, chartfold, jot)
    ↓
longecho (validate, unify, build site)
    ↓
pagevault (encrypt what needs privacy)
posthumous (ensure delivery)
    ↓
longshade (the echo)

I have never once needed to delete one of these tools. Not because I’m a better programmer than anyone else. Because each one exists for a specific reason that connects to the others. When code has purpose, dead weight doesn’t accumulate. The ecosystem stays lean because every piece is load-bearing.

This isn’t architectural foresight. It’s what happens when you build from a clear constraint. “My data has to survive without me” is a filter that works at the design stage. Every tool either serves that constraint or it doesn’t get built. There is no third category.

The Actual Skill

The most valuable skill isn’t deleting code or writing it. It’s knowing why you’re building.

If you know the purpose, code stays minimal because unnecessary code doesn’t serve it. You don’t need periodic purges. The purpose does the culling before anything gets written. Deletion is what happens when purpose was absent from the start. It’s retrospective correction for a problem that clear intent would have prevented.

I know what I’m building toward. The tools will echo after I stop maintaining them. That was the point.
